newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal PM says inflation toughest EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: Portugal PM says inflation toughest EMU goal.

text.p: Portugal has room to cut interest rates further and inflation will be the toughest target to meet for entry to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Prime Minister Antonio Guterres was quoted as saying on Wednesday.
"I believe there exists some margin for manoeuvre (in interest rates)," Guterres told Diario Economico newspaper in an interview when asked if rates could fall further.
Portugal's key repo rate has eased gradually this year to the present 7.10 percent from 8.50 percent at the start of 1996.
Asked which target was hardest to achieve to qualify to join a single European currency in 1999, Guterres said "I believe the great effort next year will be made in terms of fighting inflation."
An entry condition for EMU is that inflation can be no more than 1.5 percentage points above the average of the three best-performing countries in the 15-nation bloc.
Portugal will struggle to make the grade for EMU on inflation if it fails to keep a firm lid on wage rises, analysts said.
The 1997 pay round is underway between the government and public sector unions.
"We will have to have an extremely moderate salary policy," Guterres said.
"The negotiators know exactly what is the limit, and the margin for manoeuvre is extremely limited," Guterres said.
Unions have rejected as a "provocation" an initial government offer of 2.375 percent, which would be the mid-point of the predicted inflation rate for next year.
The government forecasts inflation between 2.25 and 2.50 percent in 1997, down from 3.25 percent this year.
Guterres said the budget deficit in 1998 should not exceed the expected deficit for 1997, targeted to fall to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product from around four percent this year.
"The intention of the government is that the deficit does not increase in 1998," Guterres said.

The government presented its 1997 budget proposals, which forecast a sharp rise in revenues and tight control of spending, to parliament on Tuesday, and the budget is expected to be passed in a vote in December.
